glyph architecture and design decisions

Source: ARCHITECTURE.md

This document explains how glyph is put together and why. It is written for contributors and for anyone curious about what happens between a pipeline and the plot in the browser.

1. The spec comes first

Building a plot produces a plain R list that describes it completely. Nothing is drawn at this stage:

glyph_spec = {
  data:      data.frame or reference
  mappings:  list of quosures (lazy, not evaluated)
  marks:     list of mark descriptors
  scales:    list of scale configs
  interact:  list of interaction configs
  animate:   animation config
  theme:     token map
  layout:    composition config
}

Most of the rest of the design follows from this. A spec can be printed, diffed and tested without rendering anything. compile() turns it into JSON that can be saved, sent to a server or embedded in a page. The spec says nothing about how it will be drawn, so a second renderer could be added without changing how plots are written. Its structure is close to Vega-Lite’s, which is what makes to_vegalite() possible.

2. Mappings are quosures

glyph(data, x = wt, y = mpg) does not evaluate wt or mpg. rlang captures each one together with the environment it was written in. Global mappings go on glyph(), and each mark can add or override its own:

glyph(mtcars, x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  mark_point(color = cyl)

Quosures are evaluated only during compile(). A mapping can be a bare column name or an expression such as log(wt) or factor(cyl), and the expression sees both the data columns and the variables around it.

3. Marks and transforms

Points, lines, bars, areas, text, rules, ribbons and links each draw the data they are given. They do not summarise it.

Statistical summaries are planned as separate, explicit steps that run on the data before it reaches a mark. None exist yet. The intended shape is:

glyph(data, x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  transform_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE) |>  # planned
  mark_ribbon(y_min = .lower, y_max = .upper) |>
  mark_line(y = .fitted)

Written this way, the path from raw data to transform to mark is visible in the code.

4. Interactions are selections

Vega-Lite treats a tooltip as a single-point selection that shows values, and glyph follows that model. A brush is an interval selection that highlights what it covers. Zoom is an interval selection on the position channels that rescales them.

glyph stores interactions in the spec, next to the marks:

interact(
  tooltip = TRUE,     # point selection, show values
  brush = TRUE,       # interval selection, highlight
  zoom = TRUE,        # interval selection, rescale
  crossfilter = TRUE  # pass the selection to linked views
)

Because they are part of the spec, interactions are kept when a plot is exported to HTML. They can be described without knowing the renderer, and a future Shiny integration could read selection events on the server.

5. Theme tokens

Colours, fonts and spacing come from a short list of named values that cascade through the plot:

font       ->  all text elements
font_size  ->  base size; title = font_size x title_size
bg         ->  plot background; fg is derived from it for contrast
fg         ->  text, axis lines, ticks
accent     ->  colour for single-series marks
grid       ->  grid visibility and colour (derived from bg)
padding    ->  all margins

Setting bg = "#1a1a2e" gives light text (fg = "#e0e0e0"), a grid colour that shows against the dark background (grid_color = "#2a2a4a") and matching tooltip styles. Tokens work the way CSS custom properties do: you change one value and everything that depends on it follows.

6. Composition

Layout is part of the spec too. compose() arranges several plots in one widget:

compose(p1, p2, p3,
        type = "wrap",
        linked_selections = TRUE,
        shared_scales = "x")

Since the layout knows about every panel, a selection in one panel can highlight rows in the others, and shared scales are computed across all panels at once. The whole layout renders as a single widget.

7. Compilation and renderers

compile() resolves mappings and scales and produces the JSON that the renderer reads. There is one renderer today:

glyph_spec --> compile() --> D3.js + SVG (htmlwidgets)
                   |
                   +--> Canvas 2D (planned)
                   +--> WebGL / regl (planned)
                   +--> static SVG / PDF export (planned)

An earlier version of compile() chose an engine (“html”, “canvas” or “webgl”) from the size of the data. Nothing downstream ever used that value, because only the D3/SVG renderer existed, so the choice had no effect. compile() now accepts only "auto" (which means "html") or "html", and rejects other engines. If a Canvas or WebGL renderer is built, it should implement the same mark, scale and interaction behaviour, with only the drawing code differing.

Known gaps

Statistical transforms. There are none yet. The plan is to start with explicit transform_*() functions for smoothing, binning, density and aggregation.

Extending glyph. A new mark needs code in both R and the JavaScript renderer, and that process is not documented yet (#9). For anything glyph can’t draw, to_vegalite() gives a starting point in Vega-Lite.

Larger datasets. Every mark is an SVG element, and there is no density rendering or way to switch off costly features (#8).

Static output. export() writes HTML and JSON only. Static SVG, PNG and PDF are planned through headless Chrome, which would keep static output identical to what the browser draws.

Technology choices

Layer Choice Rationale
R API rlang + base pipe Bare-name mappings and the native pipe R users already know
Serialization jsonlite Mature, fast, round-trips R lists to JSON cleanly
Interactive rendering htmlwidgets + D3.js v7 The standard route from R to browser graphics
Large-data rendering regl (planned) WebGL without the boilerplate; used by deck.gl
Static export headless Chrome (planned) Output matches the interactive version
Interop Vega-Lite JSON Works with R, Python (Altair) and JavaScript
